facts.raw_span: 1 day of chest pressure
subjective fevers, rhinorrhea, a dry cough, and sinus congestion
3 hours of substernal pressure that resolved spontaneously
constant chest pressure radiating to the right jaw, diaphoresis, and 1 episode of vomiting
Vital signs obtained in the Emergency Department were within normal limits
Cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm, normal point of maximum impulse without lifts, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops in supine, sitting, or standing positions
Initial serum troponin I level: 6.18 ng/mL
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
Normal sinus rhythm, ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF, ST-segment depression in lead V1, and PR-segment elevation in lead aVR
Normal coronary arteries, left ventricular end-diastolic pressure 12 mm Hg
Normal results
No medical history

concepts.why: The patient presented with chest pressure and had an elevated serum troponin I level, which is a key indicator of acute coronary syndrome.
The patient had elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, which are markers of inflammation, and the ECG findings are consistent with myocarditis.
The patient experienced vomiting and chest pressure radiating to the jaw, which are symptoms that can be associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease.
The patient had elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, which are markers of inflammation, and the ECG findings are consistent with pericarditis.
The patient experienced chest pressure radiating to the jaw, which is a symptom that can be associated with costochondritis.
The patient had a history of cough and sinus congestion, which can be symptoms of a pulmonary embolism.
The patient experienced chest pressure and vomiting, which can be symptoms of an esophageal spasm.
The patient had a history of cough and sinus congestion, which can be symptoms of acute bronchitis.
The presence of normal coronary arteries and the patient's symptoms suggest Myopericarditis, which can cause chest pressure and have normal coronary angiography results.

rationales.F01: Chest pressure is a common symptom of acute coronary syndrome and pericarditis.
rationales.F03: Substernal pressure is a common symptom of acute coronary syndrome and pericarditis.
rationales.F04: Chest pressure radiating to the jaw is a common symptom of acute coronary syndrome and pericarditis.
rationales.F07: Elevated troponin levels are a strong indicator of myocardial infarction, which is often associated with acute coronary syndrome.
rationales.F08: Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are markers of inflammation, which can be seen in myocarditis and pericarditis.
rationales.F09: ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression are a characteristic ECG finding in pericarditis.
rationales.F10: Normal coronary arteries make acute coronary syndrome less likely.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's presentation of chest pressure, ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression, and elevated inflammatory markers are more consistent with pericarditis, and the normal coronary angiography and cardiac examination results argue against acute coronary syndrome.
